extracted.intended_audience: general public, students, researchers, and musicians interested in music censorship and media regulation
extracted.subtask_description: Summarize the Parents Music Resource Center's proposals, actions, and contested criteria for identifying and labeling 'explicit' music (mid-1980s U.S. context). Includes proposed labeling schemes, categories of objectionable content, and industry/political responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Develop a voluntary music rating/labeling system
rubrics_metrics.description: Suggested a voluntary move by the RIAA and the music industry to develop music labeling in the form of a rating system similar to the film rating system developed by the Motion Picture Association of America.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Framed as voluntary industry action rather than government-imposed censorship; intended to warn parents/consumers about potentially offensive content in recordings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Printing warnings and lyrics on album covers
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposal to print warnings and lyrics on album covers to make explicit content clear to consumers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presented in contemporaneous press coverage as one of several practical steps to inform purchasers; overlaps with providing lyric sheets for labeled recordings (see PTA proposal).

rubrics_metrics.name: Restricting display/sale of explicit albums in stores
rubrics_metrics.description: Recommendation requiring record stores to put albums with explicit covers under the counters (i.e., not openly displayed for minors).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An industry/retail practice intended to limit minors' exposure and sales; some retailers reacted by outright refusing to sell labeled albums or limiting sales to adults.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pressure broadcasters not to air explicit songs/videos
rubrics_metrics.description: Suggestion to pressure television stations not to broadcast explicit songs or videos.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aimed at reducing youth exposure via broadcast media; part of a suite of actions including labeling and retail restrictions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reassess contracts of musicians for explicit/violent performance
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposal to 'reassess[ ]' the contracts of musicians who performed violently or sexually in concert.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Intended as a contractual/industry lever to discourage performances judged objectionable; raises issues about interpretation, enforcement, and artistic freedom.

rubrics_metrics.name: Create an industry panel to set standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposal to create a panel to set industry standards regarding explicit content and labeling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Would centralize definitions and guidance for labeling; the design and membership of such a panel were points of contention (who defines 'explicit'?).

rubrics_metrics.name: Categories of lyrical/content grounds for labeling (Filthy Fifteen / PTA list)
rubrics_metrics.description: Content categories cited as objectionable and grounds for labeling: sex/masturbation, sex, sex/violence, violence/language, sex, violence, sex, sex/language/violence, drug and alcohol use, occult, drug and alcohol use, sex, occult, sex/masturbation — summarized by PMRC's 'Filthy Fifteen' and PTA proposals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The PTA additionally proposed marking recordings containing 'explicit sexual language, violence, profanity, the occult and glorification of drugs and alcohol' (e.g., printing the symbol 'R'); these categories became the basis for deciding which recordings warranted warnings or restrictions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of a parental-advisory label (generic vs. descriptive)
rubrics_metrics.description: Adoption of a 'Parental Guidance: Explicit Lyrics' / 'Parental Advisory' label on albums to warn consumers of explicit lyrical content; labels were ultimately generic rather than descriptive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Industry adopted a generic advisory label (RIAA, Nov 1, 1985); the generic design contrasted with initial ideas for descriptive categories. The generic label led to varied retail responses (some stores refused to sell labeled albums or limited sales to adults). Effectiveness in preventing exposure is 'uncertain' and may produce a 'forbidden-fruit effect' that increases sales.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provision of lyrics for labeled recordings
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposal (from PTA testimony) to provide lyrics for 'R'-labeled albums so parents could review content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Intended to give parents information to make purchase decisions; raises practical questions about packaging, cost, and interpretation of lyrics out of context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Industry discretion vs. mandated labeling
rubrics_metrics.description: Debate over whether labeling should be voluntary (industry/RIAA discretion) or mandated/standardized by outside authority (Congress/official panel).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The RIAA agreed to voluntary labeling at the time; opponents argued voluntary/generic labels were inadequate and that any labeling/enforcement raises First Amendment and censorship concerns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretation and enforcement concerns (subjectivity of 'explicit')
rubrics_metrics.description: Implicit evaluative standard: labeling and censorship proposals hinge on subjective interpretations of lyrics, imagery, and intent — critics warned of misinterpretation and civil liberties infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples in hearings show artists and witnesses arguing songs were misinterpreted (e.g., Dee Snider's defense of Twisted Sister lyrics), highlighting enforcemental and interpretational problems; this serves as a caution against rigid, overbroad labeling schemes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Potential social effects and counterarguments (effectiveness and backlash)
rubrics_metrics.description: Consideration of secondary effects as a criterion: whether labels actually prevent youth exposure or instead increase interest/sales ('forbidden-fruit effect'), and whether labeling amounts to censorship counterproductive to free expression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited testimony and commentary (musicians, scholars) questioned label effectiveness and warned about censorship; policy design should weigh informational benefits against potential for increased demand and First Amendment challenges.
